reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Rehmat woke up and ran to the window. "Snow!" she said. "No school today!" Her tummy felt hungry, so she ran to the kitchen. Mama was there in her big warm sweater.

"I want to help," said Rehmat. Mama smiled. "You can watch the butter," she said. Mama put a little butter in a pan. Then Mama turned on the stove herself. Rehmat stood back and watched. The butter was hard and cold. Then it got soft. Then it turned to a shiny puddle. "It melted!" said Rehmat. "The heat did that."

Mama poured the melted butter into a bowl. "Now one egg, one splash of milk, one scoop of flour," said Mama. Rehmat counted each thing. "One, two, three!" She stirred slow, then slower, then slow again. It takes time to make pancakes.

The pancakes sizzled. Flips were Mama's job. Then, surprise, Mama made one pancake shaped like a snowman. "For my snow day kid," said Mama. Rehmat clapped. After breakfast, they looked out the window. The sun had come out. The snowman in the yard was getting small and drippy. "Look, Mama," said Rehmat. "He is melting like the butter!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story: Charles sat at the dinner table. His tummy made a little growl. "Now I am hungry," he said. "Is dinner now or later?" Mom smiled. "Later. The pot is still cooking." Dad stirred the pot on the stove. Charles stayed in his chair and watched. Steam went up, up, up. "Yesterday we had noodles," said Mom. "Today we have soup. Tomorrow we can have noodles again." Charles picked up his spoon. He tapped it on the table, one, two, three. "Can I taste now?" he asked. "Not yet," said Dad. "Hot soup must cool down." Charles wiggled one toe inside his shoe. Waiting felt long. Then Dad set the bowl on the table. A tiny curl of steam rose from it. Charles blew on the soup. Whoosh, whoosh. The steam got smaller. He took one sip. "It's not too hot now!" he said. "Yummy soup today." Mom laughed and poured milk. Charles ate his soup all up. "Tomorrow can we have it again?" he asked. "Maybe," said Dad. "But first, one bite of bread." Charles took a big, happy bite.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Raphael wanted to play house at daycare. But the baby doll was missing. Where could it be?

He looked under the table. He looked in the toy box. Then he heard a small sound. It came from the big sock pile! Raphael pulled out a thick wool sock. Something was inside it. He peeked in.

It was the baby doll, all cozy and warm. Maya had put it there for a nap. "The baby needs a blanket," Maya said. Raphael nodded. A sock could be a blanket!

He set the doll in a little basket. He patted its back, so soft. Then he made a bottle from a toy cup. He held it to the doll's mouth. Maya covered the doll with the thick sock again. The baby looked so snug.

"Time for dinner," said Raphael. He stirred a pot of toy carrots. Their teacher, Miss Jo, came to help. She held the pretend pot with two hands. "This soup smells so good," she said. Raphael smiled big.

He fed the doll one more bite. Then he wrapped the sock around it like a hug. "Sleep well, baby," he whispered.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
David woke up and saw white. The sky was full of soft snow. No school today! Dad said, "Snow day!" David wanted to sled down the big hill.

David pulled his sled up, up, up. He sat down. He pushed off. The sled did not move. It just sat in the snow. "Hmm," said David.

Dad sat on the sled too. Now it was heavy. The sled began to slide. Down, down they went. Whee! "Again," said David. He climbed the hill again.

They went down and down. Then David was cold. His mittens were wet. Mom had hot cocoa waiting. She was careful with the hot cup. David blew and blew on his cocoa. He sipped it slow. Outside, the snow fell on the hill, ready for tomorrow. "More sledding tomorrow," said David. Dad smiled and said, "Yes, tomorrow."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Elizabeth went to the park with her dad. She saw a big round swing. A boy was on it. "I want a turn," she said. Dad said, "We can ask." Elizabeth waited by the fence. She counted the flowers while she waited. Soon the boy jumped off. "Your turn," he said. Elizabeth sat on the swing. Dad pushed her high. She laughed and laughed.

Next they went to the sand pit. Two kids were there. They had one red shovel. Elizabeth had a small blue bucket. "I can share my bucket," she said. The girl gave her the shovel. They dug a round hole together. It was big enough for both hands.

Then a teacher blew a whistle. All the kids ran to the benches. Elizabeth ran too. Everyone sat in a line. A grown-up handed out little cakes from a basket. Each child got one cake. Elizabeth took hers. "We all got the same," she said. She bit into her cake. It was sweet.

Dad sat close by on the bench. Elizabeth leaned on his arm. "One more swing," she said, "and then we go home." Dad smiled and held her hand.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Emily sat in her car seat. She was hungry. "Mom, do you have a snack?"

Mom reached into the bag. "Let's look. I see an apple. The apple is a food."

Emily took a bite. Crunch! Then she looked out the window.

A cow stood by the fence. "Look, a cow! The cow is an animal," said Emily.

Next came a big truck. It was full of soft teddy bears. "Toys!" said Emily. "So many toys!"

Then the truck hit a bump. A teddy bear fell out. It bounced on the road. Dad stopped the car, very slow and safe.

Dad picked up the teddy bear. He knocked on the truck window. The driver looked back. He saw his teddy bear. He laughed and waved.

"You saved my teddy bear!" he said.

A little spider sat on the teddy bear's ear. It waved too, or maybe that was just the wind.

Emily giggled. "Mom, can we get a teddy bear too?"

Mom smiled. "Maybe at the next stop."

Emily hugged her apple and waited for the next window surprise.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. Bennett wanted to make him feel happy at home. "What does Grandpa like?" Mom asked. "Tea!" said Bennett. So they went to the market. Bennett found a big red apple. He found a loaf of fresh bread. Then he saw a little tin of tea. "Grandpa can try this," he said.

At home, Mom put water in the kettle. She made it hot, and Bennett stood back. Mom dropped the tea bag in the cup. Bennett watched. The water began to turn brown. First it was light brown. Then it was dark brown. "It changed!" said Bennett. Mom poured in a little milk. The tea turned creamy.

Grandpa took a sip. "Mmm," he said. "You picked my favorite." Bennett grinned. Tomorrow he would try the red apple trick too.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Ayla ran into the school cafeteria. It was her first day of school! She looked for a seat. She wanted a friend to sit with.

One girl sat alone. She had a smelly tuna sandwich. Ayla saw the girl take a big bite. Then the girl's tummy made a loud rumble. "My tummy talks when I eat!" the girl said. Ayla laughed and sat down.

Ayla opened her lunch. "I have a apple, a banana, and crackers," she said. "One, two, three!" She took a big bite of her apple. Her tummy made a rumble too! The girl laughed this time. "I know that sound," said Ayla. "Winter is coming and my tummy is hungry!" The two girls counted their snacks together. Then they shared one cracker each. "Same seat tomorrow?" asked the girl. "Yes!" said Ayla, and she clapped her hands.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Sarah wanted to make a flower picture. She sat at the big table. Mom put down paper and glue.

Sarah found some paper petals. She put glue on a petal. She pressed it down. She lifted her finger. The petal came up too! It was stuck to her skin. "Oh no," said Sarah. "My petal will not stay."

Mom sat close by her. "Try pressing it longer," said Mom. Sarah pressed the petal again. She counted to three in her head. She lifted her finger slowly. This time the petal stayed on the paper. Sarah clapped her hands.

She glued more petals, one by one. She pressed each one and waited. Each petal stayed. Then she glued a yellow circle for the middle. Her flower was done.

Sarah held up her paper. "A flower for you!" she said. Mom smiled and put it on the fridge. Sarah looked at her sticky fingers. They felt yucky and stiff. "Wash time," said Mom. They washed their hands with warm, soapy water. The water ran bubbly and soft over Sarah's fingers.

Then Mom took Sarah's hand. They walked out to see the real flowers in the garden. A big red one nodded in the wind. "It looks like my picture," said Sarah.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Billie waited at the bus stop with her mother. The sun was out. It was sunny and hot. Billie took off her hat. "Where should I put it?" she asked. Her mother put the hat in the bag. The bus was coming soon.

Then the wind blew. It was windy! The wind pushed Billie's dress. It made the leaves dance. The wind pushed a paper cup along the ground. Billie laughed and chased the cup. The wind pushed it again. Billie saw that the wind moved things.

Then big drops fell. It was rainy! "Where is the rain going?" Billie asked. "On my head," said her mother. Her mother opened a thick umbrella. The rain went plip, plop on top. Billie stayed dry under it. Billie's puppy drank rain from a little puddle.

Then white flakes came down. It was snowy! Billie stuck out her tongue. A flake landed on it. The bus came at last. Billie and her mother climbed on. Billie waved at the snow through the big window. "Look, puppy, snow!" said Billie.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Maeve sat on the bus with her dad. She looked in her bag. "Bunny is gone!" she said. "Oh no," said Dad. "Let's look for bunny."

Maeve looked under the seat. She saw a crayon. But no bunny. She looked by her feet. The bus went around a corner. Her crayon rolled away! The crayon rolled straight under the big seat ahead. Maeve leaned down and peeked.

"Mommy, look!" said a small boy. He was holding a soft white bunny. It had been sitting under his seat. "That is my bunny," said Maeve. "Thank you for catching him," said Dad. The boy smiled and gave bunny back. Maeve hugged bunny tight. "I found you," she whispered. Bunny's ears tickled her chin, and she giggled all the way home.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Snow was falling outside the daycare window. The sky was gray and soft. Ryan pressed his nose to the cold glass.

Miss Pam rang the little bell. "Snack time," she said. "Ryan, can you bring cups? We need ten."

Ryan went to the shelf. He took one cup. "One," he said. He took another. "Two." He put them on his arm. He kept taking cups. "Three, four, five." Miss Pam began to hum a counting song. The other kids sang too. "Six, seven, eight." Ryan hummed along. He took more cups. "Nine, ten!"

He carried the cups to the table. But then the stack wobbled. The cups tipped over and rolled. Ryan picked them up one at a time. "One, two, three," he said, setting them down. Each cup got a number name. "Four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Every chair had a cup by it. Nothing rolled away this time.

Miss Pam smiled. "Ten cups for ten friends." Ryan sat down. He wore his snack bib with the red truck on it. He munched his crackers and looked at the snow.

"Ten crackers left," said his friend Ben, counting his plate. Ryan laughed and counted his too.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Lily put her cold milk cup on the table. "One cup, two carrots, three crackers," she said. She touched the cup. It was cold. She wanted it warm.

Ms. Rosa took the cup. She put it in a big machine. Lily watched from her little chair. The machine made a hum. It was fast. The cup went round and round.

Lily held a letter block. It was the letter L, for Lily. Her friend Sam held a small block. Hers was big. His was small. They stacked them up, big one first, then small one on top.

The machine stopped. Ms. Rosa brought the cup back. "Careful now," she said. "It is warm." Lily touched the side. It was warm, not cold anymore. The big machine made it warm, and the fast hum told her when it was done.

At the art table, Sam dipped his brush. He painted a red line, slow and slow. Lily painted a fast line, quick quick quick. The paint felt slimy on her fingers. She laughed.

"Snack time," Ms. Rosa called. Lily did not shout. She walked. She picked up her warm cup. One sip, two sips. "Warm milk," she said. Sam smiled at her over his big cracker.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Gabriel wanted to build a house for his teddy bear. He looked for shapes all over the house. He found a round plate. "A circle!" he said. He found a book with four sides the same. "A square!" He found a slice of bread with two long sides. "A rectangle!"

But he had no roof. Teddy's head was cold. Gabriel looked and looked. Then he saw Daddy folding a napkin. Daddy folded it corner to corner. The napkin made a triangle, with three pointy sides. "A triangle roof!" Gabriel said.

Gabriel put the circle under teddy for a rug. He made square walls from blocks. The rectangle was teddy's little bed. The triangle went on top. Teddy sat inside. Gabriel clapped his hands. The clap was loud. Teddy fell over, and Gabriel caught him with one arm. "Got you," Gabriel said. "No falling out of your new house."

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Madison went to the library with her dad. The floor was shiny and a little slippery. She walked carefully.

She wanted the duck book. It was about ducks at the park. But the book sat on a high shelf. "How can I reach it?" she asked. Dad brought a little stool. "Try this," he said. Madison stepped up. The stool made her taller. Now her hand could touch the book. She pulled it down all by herself.

Then story time began. The librarian sang a song. "One, two, three, four, five," she sang. The children clapped. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Madison clapped too. She counted ducks on her lap. "One, two, three," she said. She tapped each duck as she said a number. Each tap matched one duck.

"How many ducks are there?" she asked Dad. They counted together. "Ten ducks," said Dad. Madison thought about that. Ten was a big number for such a small book.

At the desk, Dad helped her check the book out. The librarian stamped it. "Ten days," she said. Madison hugged the book tight and waved goodbye to the ducks.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Charlotte wanted to paint with her big brother, Sam. Sam had one red brush. Charlotte had one blue brush. But Sam had all the yellow paint.

"I want some yellow," said Charlotte. Sam looked at his cup. He poured some yellow into her cup. Charlotte painted a big sun. Sam painted a bee on the sun. The bee looked happy.

Then Charlotte grabbed Sam's paper. She wanted to paint on it too. Sam said, "Give it back. That one is mine." Charlotte gave it back slowly. Mom brought a new sheet. "Here is one for you," said Mom. Charlotte painted a fat, sleepy cat. The cat looked asleep under the sun. Sam laughed. "Nice cat," he said. "Now we can hang them side by side." Charlotte held up her painting next to his.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Sarah wanted to wash her hands all by herself. Dad stood in the doorway. "Can I turn the water?" she asked. "I will help," Dad said.

Sarah reached for the tap. Dad put his hand on top. "Let me turn the hot side," he said. Dad turned it a little. Steam came up. Sarah put her hand near it. "Ooh, it is warm like soup," she said. Dad turned the cold side. The steam went away. Sarah touched the water. It felt nice and cool now.

Then Sarah saw Dad's razor on the sink. It was shiny. She reached out. "Not that one," Dad said quickly. He moved it far away. "That is for grown-ups only." Sarah pulled her hand back. She looked at Dad. "Okay," she said.

Sarah washed her hands with soap. She made bubbles. She counted them, one, two, three. "I did it!" she said. Dad clapped. "Good job, Sarah." Sarah dried her hands on the old blue towel. "Can we wash again tomorrow?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad. "We can wash every day." Sarah smiled and hung the towel on its hook.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Emilia woke up in her sunny bed. She wanted to help in the kitchen today. First she needed to get dressed. She pulled her red shirt on all by herself. It was backwards, but Mama smiled and helped her fix it.

In the kitchen, Mama made warm oatmeal. Emilia helped stir. She stirred and stirred, and the oatmeal got thick. Then she ate it all up. "Yum," she said. After eating, Emilia dropped some oatmeal on the floor. Papa got the broom. Emilia held the dustpan. Papa helped her sweep the crumbs into it. The floor was clean again.

Then Emilia heard the bath water run. It splashed and bubbled. Mama felt the water with her hand. "Just right," said Mama. Emilia washed her toes and her tummy. After the bath, she put on her soft pajamas. She yawned a big yawn. Papa read her one story. Emilia hugged her bear and fell fast asleep.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Elijah sat in the big salon chair. It was his first haircut ever. The chair was too tall, so Mommy held his hand. Elijah wanted to see what the lady would do.

The lady picked up her comb. She combed his hair up, up, up. Then she snipped with her scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Little bits of hair fell down. They landed on the cape like dark snow.

"Look," said Elijah. "My hair came off!"

The lady laughed. "The comb lifts it. Then the scissors cut it. That is how my work goes."

She combed again. Snip, snip. More dark bits fell. Elijah patted the cape. The bits slid off his hand. He giggled.

Then the lady turned the chair to the mirror. Elijah looked. His hair was short now!

"My head looks small," he said.

"Your head looks just right," said Mommy.

The lady brushed his neck with a soft brush. It tickled. Elijah wiggled like a worm.

She held up the mirror in back. Elijah saw the back of his own head. He waved at it. The boy in the mirror waved back.

"That works," said Elijah. "Two of me!"

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Zoey wanted to make a special picture for Gran. She needed stickers. She had only one star sticker. One was not enough.

Mom brought a big sheet. "Let's count the stars," said Mom. Zoey pointed. "One, two, three." Mom pointed too. "Four, five, six." Zoey touched each star. "Seven, eight, nine." One star was left in the corner. "Ten!" said Zoey. She smiled.

Zoey peeled the stars slowly. Some stars stuck to her finger. She tried again. Stick, press, smooth. The stars went on the paper one by one. At last the picture was done. Zoey held it up high. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten stars for Gran!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Grace held her mama's hand in the school hallway. The hall was long. Grace could not see her classroom door.

"Where is my room?" said Grace.

"Look at the doors," said Mama. "Each door has a picture."

Grace saw a door with a cat. She saw a door with a sun. Then she saw a door with a red balloon, just like the red balloon on her bag.

Grace let go of the balloon. It floated up and bumped the door with the cat. That was not her door. Grace pulled it back down. "Silly balloon," she said.

She walked on. The balloon bumped the door with a sun. Not that door either. Grace pulled it back again. "Silly, silly balloon," said Mama, laughing.

Then the balloon floated up to the red balloon door. It bumped the picture. A teacher opened the door. "Hello, Grace," she said. "We have been waiting for you."

Grace stepped in and found a little chair with her name on it. She sat down and waved. "Bye, Mama! This is my last stop!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Milan went to the park with his toy elephant. He put it down by the bench. Then he ran to the slide. When he came back, the elephant was gone.

"Where did it go?" said Milan. He looked with his eyes. He saw grass, rocks and a red ball. He listened with his ears. He heard birds and a dog barking. He sniffed with his nose. He smelled popcorn near the swings. He touched the grass with his hands. It was soft and a little wet.

His mom said, "Follow your nose." Milan walked toward the popcorn smell. He saw his elephant under the snack cart. A girl was holding it. "Is this yours?" she asked. "Yes! I know that elephant anywhere," said Milan. He hugged it. "You are a lucky elephant," he said. "And I found you with my eyes, my ears, my nose and my hands."

The girl laughed. "Want one thing more?" she said. She held out a small cup. Her dad had bought warm popcorn for everyone. Milan ate one piece with his mouth. It was salty and good. He munched and smiled. "Best park day ever," he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Maria sat on the small bench at Miss Penny's music studio. She wanted to make music like Miss Penny did. But the big drum would not make a sound for her.

"Tap it," said Miss Penny. "Soft hands first."

Maria tapped soft. The drum made a tiny sound. Tap, tap, tap. It was small like a mouse.

"Now tap hard," said Miss Penny.

Maria lifted her hand and tapped hard. BOOM! The drum made a big sound. It was big like a lion!

Maria tapped soft. Tiny sound. She tapped hard. BOOM!

"My hands make it loud!" said Maria. She tapped soft, then hard, soft, then hard.

Miss Penny laughed. "Yes. Your hands are in charge."

Maria wanted one more big boom. She tapped hard with both hands. BOOM! BOOM!

The window shook a little. The room felt warm, like the sun had come in. Maria thought the drum might feel hot from so much noise.

"Drums can build a big song," said Miss Penny. "Tap with me."

They tapped together. Soft, soft, BOOM! Soft, soft, BOOM!

Maria tapped her knees. Then she clapped her hands. Then she reached up for the drum one more time.

"BOOM!" she said, and tapped again.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Abigail looked out the window. Snow was everywhere! School was closed today. "Snow day!" said Mom.

Abigail put on her boots. Her coat was red. Her mittens were wide and puffy. She and Mom walked to the park. The snow went crunch, crunch under her boots.

Abigail wanted to make a snowball. She scooped up snow. She pressed it with her mittens. But the snow would not stick. It fell apart in a pile. "Oh no," said Abigail.

"Try the sticky snow by the slide," said Mom. "The sun sat on it. It got warm and squishy."

Abigail scooped snow by the slide. She pressed it. It stuck! She made a big round snowball. Then she made a little one on top. "A snow frog!" said Abigail. She clapped her mittens.

The snow frog sat on the slide. Abigail smiled wide. "More snow!" she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Ivy sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. She was a little scared of the check-up. Her tummy felt jumpy.

The doctor came in with a smile. "Ivy, can you be my helper today?" she asked. "We are a team." Ivy nodded. First the doctor held up a small picture. "Tell me what you see." Ivy looked with her eyes. "A duck!" she said. Next the doctor tapped a little bell. Ivy heard it with her ears. "It rings!" Then the doctor held something soft. Ivy touched it with her fingers. "It feels like my teddy," she said. The doctor had a sticker that smelled like strawberries. Ivy sniffed with her nose. "It smells sweet!" Last, the doctor gave her a safe taste strip. Ivy put it on her tongue. "It tastes like nothing," she said, and she laughed.

"Good helper," said the doctor. "Now pick a bandaid." Ivy chose a shiny one with stars. She pressed it on with her finger. "My eyes saw this one," she said proudly. The doctor gave her a high five.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Kayden ran to the big sports field. Papa held his hand. "The game starts soon!" said Papa.

Kayden sat on the grass with Mama and Nia. Lots of people came to watch. The players ran and kicked the ball. The crowd clapped and cheered.

But then the wind blew hard. The wind pushed a big paper flag. The flag fell down, flop! Kayden stood up. "The wind did that!" he said.

Kayden picked up the flag. He held it up high. The wind blew again. The flag went flap, flap, flap. When the wind stopped, the flag hung still.

Papa laughed. "Hold it tight, Kayden." Kayden held it tight. He waved it when the wind came. The crowd saw the flag flapping. They cheered even louder.

The weather was not bad at all now. The sun came out. The players kicked the ball into the net. "Goal!" everyone shouted.

Kayden waved his flag. It was the best game ever. "Again! Again!" he said. Papa said, "Next week we come back." Kayden smiled big. The flag went flap, flap, flap one more time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Isaac wanted to make pancakes for his family. He found a bowl and a spoon. His dad said, "I will pour the milk. You can stir."

Isaac stirred and stirred. Then he dropped in a few blueberries. One blueberry sat on top. It would not sink.

"Why won't it go down?" Isaac asked.

Dad smiled. "Stir harder and see."

Isaac stirred fast. The blueberry popped under the batter. Now it was hiding inside. Isaac laughed. "I made it hide!"

Dad poured circles onto the hot pan. Isaac watched from his stool. The pancakes got little bubbles on top. "Look, Dad! Bubbles!"

"That means they are ready to flip," said Dad.

He flipped one high in the air. It landed with a plop. Isaac clapped his hands.

The pancakes went onto a red plate. Mom and the baby came out to the backyard table. Everyone ate and ate.

"The best pancakes ever," said Mom.

Isaac grinned. "I hid the blueberries!"

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Luke ran into the storytime room. He was going to get his very own library card! The librarian smiled at him. "Say your name," she said. "Luke!" he said, loud and round like a drum. She typed his name. Then she gave him a card with a red bird on it. Luke held it with both hands.

"Can I pick a book?" Luke asked. "Yes," said Mom. "You can take it home." Luke found a book about a seed that grows into a big sunflower. "I want to keep it forever!" he said.

The librarian shook her head. "You have to bring it back," she said. "Other kids want to read it too." Luke hugged the book tight. Then he saw a girl looking at the sunflower book. She wanted it too. Luke handed the book to the librarian. "I'll bring it back soon," he said. The girl waved at him. Luke waved back, holding his new card up high.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Violet was on the swim team. Today was the big pool day. She put on her little red swimsuit. "Kick, kick, kick," said Coach Amy.

Violet sat on the edge. She wanted to splash the farthest. She kicked her legs in the water. Splash! It was a small splash. The water felt cool on her toes.

Then Violet watched Ben. Ben was bigger. He moved his whole legs up and down. His splash went way out. It even hit the wall!

Violet wondered about that. She tried a big kick with her whole leg. Up and down, up and down. Splash! The water flew far. "Look at me!" she called. Coach Amy clapped. "Nice big kick, Violet!"

Ben gave her a thumbs up. Violet kicked again. Up and down, up and down. The water splashed all the way to Ben. He laughed and splashed her back. "Got you!" said Violet.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Everly went to the big library with her dad. She held his hand in the reading room. Today she would get her very own library card.

"Can I keep the book forever?" Everly asked.

"Let's ask the library lady," said Dad.

The library lady smiled. "You can take it home," she said. "Then you bring it back on this day." She pointed to a stamp inside the book.

Everly picked a book about a cow who could blow big bubbles. She carried it to the desk. The lady scanned her new card. Beep!

At home, Everly read the book four times. She read it to her teddy bear. The cow blew a bubble as big as a room.

Then the day on the stamp came. Everly gave the book back to Dad. They took it to the library together.

"Someone else can read about my cow now," Everly said. "And I can get a new book!"

She skipped to the shelf, and the library lady said, "Back already? You are quick!"

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Mackenzie put on her red birthday shoe. One shoe was red and one was blue. "Silly shoes!" said Daddy. Everyone laughed.

It was Mackenzie's birthday party at the bowling alley. Grandma, Grandpa, and her friend Nora came too. Mackenzie wanted to knock down the pins. All ten pins!

She picked a little blue ball. She pushed it with both hands. The ball went slow. Then the ball went into the gutter. No pins fell down. "Oh no," said Mackenzie.

"Try again," said Nora. Nora rolled her ball. Her ball went straight. It hit the pins. Crash! The pins fell down. Mackenzie watched. The ball hit one pin. That pin fell over. Then it bumped the next pin. That pin fell too. One pin made another pin fall!

Mackenzie took her turn again. She pushed her ball hard. It rolled down the middle. It hit the big pin. That pin tipped. It knocked three more pins. "Strike!" shouted Grandpa. "One pin helped the ball!" said Mackenzie.

After bowling, they ate pizza. The popcorn was salty and yummy. Then Daddy carried out the cake. He lit the candles, all safe. Mackenzie blew and blew. Out went every candle. "Happy birthday, dear Mackenzie!" everyone sang.

Then Grandma brought out one more box. It had a bow on top. "For the birthday girl," said Grandma. Mackenzie opened it. Inside was her very own little bowling pin.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story: Zayn ran out to the baseball diamond. He wanted to hit the ball far. His coach tossed the ball. Zayn swung the bat. He slipped in the dirt and fell on his bottom. "Ouch," said Zayn. His teammate Ben laughed, but not in a mean way. "The dirt is loose here," said Ben. "Watch me." Ben dug his shoes into the dirt. He made two deep little holes for his feet. Then Ben swung. He did not slip. The ball went far, far away. Zayn stood up. "Can I try that too?" he asked. "Sure," said Ben. Zayn dug his shoes in. He made his own deep holes. He swung the bat. No slip! The ball rolled all the way to the fence. "Again!" said Zayn, and dug his feet in one more time.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Emily had a library book about a bunny. The bunny had soft, curly fur on the cover. Emily wanted to keep the book forever.

At bedtime, Dad said, "Tomorrow we take the book back. It is due. Other kids want to read about the bunny too." Emily held the book tight. "Can we read it one more time?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad.

Dad opened the front cover. "See the words?" he said. "They say the bunny's name." Emily looked. The marks on the page meant something. Dad turned the pages one by one, front to back. The bunny found a carrot at the end.

The next day, Emily gave the book back. Then the library lady smiled. "Look," she said. "The bunny has a new book, and you can borrow it too." Emily hugged the new book. "I will remember to bring it back," she said. On the way home, the cool air tickled her face. She held the new book all the way.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Beatrice woke up and looked out the window. The world was white! No school today. "Snow day!" said Mama.

Beatrice wanted to sled down the big hill. But her sled would not go. It just sat there. Papa pushed her sled. It still did not move. "Too much snow is soft," said Papa with a smile.

Then Beatrice saw Papa stomp on the snow. His boots made the snow flat. The flat part was shiny and hard. "Stomp, stomp, stomp!" said Beatrice. She stomped her little boots too. They made a path all the way down the hill.

Beatrice sat on her sled. Papa gave one push. Zoom! The sled went fast on the flat, shiny path. "Faster!" laughed Beatrice. "Wheee!"

After sledding, they went home. Mama made cocoa. A snow worm poked out of a pile by the door. "Hello, different little friend," said Beatrice. She pretended to feed the snow worm a pretend cookie. Then she took a big sip. "Warm tummy," said Beatrice. "More sledding tomorrow!"

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Rowan was hungry. He looked in his toy basket. "No snack here," he said. "Just my ball and my truck." Dad was grilling lunch in the yard. Rowan wanted to help find the food.

A bird hopped by the fence. Then a squirrel came too. The squirrel found a nut on the ground. It held the nut and ate it. Rowan watched. The squirrel looked in one place and found food. So Rowan could look too.

He ran to the little cooler by the table. He opened the lid. There were apples and cheese inside. "Dad! I found the foods!" he called. Dad smiled and handed him a cold apple from the frozen ice pack spot. Rowan took a big bite. The squirrel ran up the tree with its nut.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Everly sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. She wanted a sticker, but first she had to wait. "Can I have a sticker now?" she asked. "Not yet," said Mom. "First the doctor will look at you."

The nurse came in. She held a small light. "Can you follow the light with your eyes?" she asked. Everly's eyes watched the light go up and down. The nurse smiled. Then the nurse tapped Everly's knee. Everly's leg jumped all by itself. "Why did my leg do that?" Everly asked. "It jumps when you tap it," said the nurse. Everly tapped her own knee. The leg jumped again. She laughed.

Next the doctor came. He looked in Everly's ears. He looked in her nose. He looked in her mouth. "Say ahh," he said. Everly said, "Ahh." Then he gave her a little stick to press with her finger. It felt soft and bumpy.

Then the nurse gave Everly a cookie. Everly smelled it first. It smelled sweet. She took a bite. It tasted good. "You used your nose and your tongue," said the nurse. "Where is my sticker?" Everly asked. The nurse put a shiny star sticker on her hand. Everly touched it with one finger. It was smooth. "Star!" she said.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Livia could not find her bunny. Bunny had one floppy ear and a pink bow. She looked under the table. No bunny. She looked in the dress-up box. No bunny.

Miss Anna sat down next to her. "Tell me where you played today," she said. Livia began to speak. "I played at the sand table. Then I read books on the big rug." Miss Anna smiled. "Let's look there."

Livia shook the rug. The rug made a soft whoosh. Something small rolled out from under it. It was a toy coin from the money tin! Then Livia spotted a pink ear sticking out too.

"Bunny!" she cried. She picked bunny up and hugged her tight.

"How did bunny get there?" Livia asked. Miss Anna laughed. "The rug was hiding her."

Livia put the coin back in the tin. She held bunny's paw all the way to snack time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Anna was afraid of the big drum. It sat in the band room. It was as tall as her tummy.

"I want to bang it," said Anna. "But it looks too big."

Mr. Pip held out a small drum. "Try this one," he said. "Tap it soft."

Anna tapped one finger. The drum made a tiny sound. Tappity.

Anna tapped harder. The drum made a big sound. BOOM!

Anna jumped. Then she laughed. "My hand did that!"

She tapped soft again. Tappity. She tapped big again. BOOM!

"Now you know your drum," said Mr. Pip. "Soft hands, small sound. Big hands, big sound."

Anna played a song. Tappity, BOOM, BOOM, tappity.

Tommy covered his ears. "Too loud!"

Anna tapped soft for Tommy. Tappity, tappity.

"Better," said Tommy.

After band, the teacher gave out cookies. Anna held her cookie up like a drumstick.

"Don't you dare," said Mr. Pip.

BOOM went the crumbs on the table. Anna laughed and ate her drumstick cookie all up.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Jaxon ran to the red slide at the park. A girl was already at the top. "My turn next," she called down. Jaxon stopped and waited. He watched her zoom down, fast. Could waiting be worth it? He thought maybe it could. "Your turn now," the girl said. "You waited, so you go." Jaxon climbed up the ladder. He slid down, and the wind rushed past his ears. Whee!

Next Jaxon found the sandbox. A boy had all the trucks. Three trucks, and only one boy. Jaxon wanted a truck so much. "Can I have one?" Jaxon asked. The boy looked at his trucks. Then he pushed a blue truck across the sand. "Here," the boy said. "You take this one." They made a big sand hill together. Two trucks made a bigger hill than one truck. Jaxon noticed that.

Then Jaxon saw a small pond. A turtle sat on a rock in the sun. A sign stood by the water. Jaxon's dad read it out loud. "The sign says we stay out of the pond." Jaxon nodded. Then a dog ran by and jumped in. Splash! The turtle slipped off the rock. The turtle swam away under the water. "Bye bye, turtle," Jaxon said. He waved at the rock.

On the way home, Jaxon held his dad's strong hand. He looked back at the slide. Kids were going down, one by one. One by one, like a line of little ants. "Can we come back tomorrow?" Jaxon asked. "Yes," said Dad. "We can come back tomorrow."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
It was Jayden's birthday at the park. His mom put four candles on the cake. Grandpa lit them with a match. Jayden watched from his spot.

"Make a wish," said Mom. "Then blow."

Jayden blew. The little flames bent. But they came back up. He blew again, harder. The flames went out, all four.

"How did they go out?" Jayden asked.

"My wind did it," said his sister, Nia. "Watch." She puffed, and her one candle went dark too.

Then the wind in the trees blew. The napkins lifted off the table. But the candles stayed out. No flames came back.

"One candle, two candles, three candles, four," said Grandma. "All done."

Jayden laughed. "The wind outside is strong like my wind!"

He cut the air with his hand, whoosh, whoosh. Nia clapped. Then everyone sang the birthday song, and Jayden blew one more time, at nothing at all, just for fun.
